standard.title: Navigate print and screen texts
standard.description: navigate print and screen texts using chapters, tables of contents, indexes, side-bar menus, drop-down menus or links
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how print and screen texts are organised using navigation and structural features such as page numbers, headings and links (AC9E1LA05). They have not yet actively navigated these features to locate specific information — their prior knowledge is understanding how features work, not using them purposefully.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can navigate print and screen texts using chapters, tables of contents, indexes, side-bar menus, drop-down menus and links to locate specific information.

nodes.label: How print navigation features work
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how chapters, tables of contents and indexes are organised to support information access — numbering, alphabetical order, page reference — and use at least one to locate information.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a table of contents to locate a specific chapter or section in a non-fiction book.
nodes.typical_width: Use tables of contents, chapters and indexes across several non-fiction books; explain how numbered chapters and alphabetical indexes are organised to support access; use an index to locate a specific term.
wider: Compare the organisation of indexes across two different non-fiction books and discuss why some terms are included and others are not
Create a simple table of contents for a class-made information text, making decisions about chapter sequence
success_criteria: Student can use a table of contents to locate a chapter and an index to locate a specific term.
Student can explain how the alphabetical order of an index speeds up information retrieval.

nodes.label: How digital navigation features work
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use website navigation tools — side-bar menus, drop-down menus and links — to locate information on a familiar website.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a side-bar menu or navigation link on a familiar website to locate a specific piece of information.
nodes.typical_width: Explore navigation tools on different websites — side-bar menus, drop-down menus, links, search bars — and explain how each tool helps users locate information.
wider: Compare the navigation structures of two different websites with similar purposes (e.g. two library or museum sites) and discuss which is easier to use and why
Identify how navigation menus on mobile and desktop versions of the same site differ
success_criteria: Student can use at least one digital navigation feature to locate specified information.
Student can name the navigation feature they used and explain what it does.

nodes.label: Choosing the right navigation tool
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select the appropriate navigation tool — print or digital — for a given information retrieval task and explain their choice.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a specific information-finding task, identify whether an index, table of contents or a website menu is the most efficient tool to use.
nodes.typical_width: Compare print and digital navigation tools and discuss when each is more efficient; navigate both types to locate information for a purpose and reflect on the experience.
wider: Compare information retrieval using a print index vs a website search bar for the same topic, and discuss the trade-offs
Explore how accessibility features (text-to-speech, screen-reader navigation) change how digital navigation works for different users

response_modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of print and digital navigation tools and applies them to a purposeful retrieval task. Coordinating knowledge of both tool types to make an informed choice is the new cognitive demand.

success_criteria: Student can select an appropriate navigation tool for a given task and explain why they chose it.
Student can use both a print and a digital navigation feature to locate specific information.
